en: Oṃ! May He protect us both; may He nourish us both;
may we work together with vigor.
May our study be full of splendor;
may we not harbor mutual hatred.
Om! Peace! Peace! Peace!
The First Chapter. Hari Om. Those who discourse on Brahman say:
What is the cause? What is Brahman? From where have we been born? By what do we live? And wherein are we established?
By whom are we, the knowers of Brahman, governed as we abide in the states of pleasure and its opposite? Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.1.
Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, and the person—these are to be considered.
It is the conjunction of these [that causes the world], and not from the self's own being; for the self, too, is not the master over the cause of pleasure and pain. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.2)

Following the yoga of meditation, they beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities—that One who alone presides over all those causes when they are joined with Time and the Self. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.3)

It has one rim, is threefold, ends in sixteen, and has fifty spokes; it has twenty counter-spokes, six sets of eight, a single noose of manifold forms, a division into three paths, two signs, and a single delusion. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.4)
We meditate upon that river which has five currents of water, five fierce crocodiles in the form of the five wombs, five waves of the vital breaths, and its source in the five faculties of cognition;
it has five whirlpools, the force of the flood of the five miseries, fifty divisions, and five stages. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.5)
In this vast wheel of Brahman, which is the source of all livelihoods and the foundation of all things, the *haṃsa* (the individual soul) revolves.
Having perceived the Self as distinct from the Impeller, and being thus favored by Him, one attains immortality. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.6)
This supreme Brahman is indeed sung as the Udgītha; in it are established the three and the Imperishable.
Having realized the interval therein, those who know Brahman, being devoted to it, merge into Brahman and are liberated from the womb. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.7)
The Lord sustains this entire universe—the perishable and the imperishable, the manifest and the unmanifest—joined together.
Yet the self, though not the Lord, is bound by its state as an enjoyer; but by knowing God, it is released from all fetters. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.8)

The two, the Knower and the Unknowing, the Lord and the Non-Lord—the Unborn is indeed one, joined with the objects of the enjoyer and the enjoyed; and the infinite Self is of universal form, for it is a non-doer. When one perceives these three as this Brahman, [one attains liberation]. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.9)
The perishable is Pradhāna; the imperishable immortal is Hara. The one God rules over both the perishable and the self.
Through meditation upon Him, through union with Him, and through becoming His true essence, there occurs at the end the cessation of the universal illusion. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10)
Having known God, there is the falling away of all bonds; with the afflictions exhausted, there is the abandonment of birth and death.
Through intense meditation upon Him, upon the dissolution of the body, one attains absolute sovereignty over all things, being solitary and having all desires fulfilled. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.11)
This is to be known as eternally established in the Self; indeed, there is nothing further to be known beyond this.
Having understood the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—all this is declared to be the threefold Brahman. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.12)
Just as the form of fire, when it has entered its source, is not seen and yet its characteristic sign is not destroyed,
and it is later perceived again when taken from its source of fuel— so too are both of these [the individual soul and the supreme self] in the body by means of the *praṇava*.

Making one's own body the lower friction-stick and the *praṇava* the upper friction-stick, by the practice of churning through meditation, one beholds the God as if hidden. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.14)

As oil is in sesame seeds, as butter is in curds, as water is in riverbeds, and as fire is in the two kindling woods—so is that Self grasped within the self by one who perceives it through truth and austerity. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.15)
The Self, which pervades all, is contained within like butter in milk;
that supreme Brahman, whose root is the knowledge of the Self and austerity, is the Upaniṣad. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.16)
"That Brahman is the supreme Upaniṣad.
Thus ends the first chapter;
here begins the second chapter.
Yoking the mind first for the sake of truth, Savitṛ, having perceived the light of Agni, brought it forth from the earth. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.1)

[*1] This mantra is also found in Yajurveda 11.1. "With a disciplined mind, we, through the impulse of the god Savitṛ, by our power, for the sake of going to the heavenly world... [*2] ... // ŚvetUp 2.2 //
[*2] This mantra is also found in Yajurveda 11.2:
"Having yoked the gods with the mind, as they go toward heaven with their thought, may Savitṛ impel them as they are about to produce the great light. [*3] Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.3.

This mantra is also found in the *Yajurveda* 11.3: “The inspired ones harness the mind and they harness the thoughts of the great, inspired, wise one. He alone, knowing the ways, ordains the priestly functions. Great indeed is the praise of the god Savitṛ. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.4)
[*4] This mantra is also found in Yajurveda 11.4, 5.14, and Ṛgveda 5.81.1.
I yoke for you both the ancient prayer with prostrations; may the fame of the wise one go forth like along the path.
May all the sons of immortality hear it, they who have taken up their stations in the celestial realms. [*5] (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.5)
This mantra is also found in the *Yajurveda* 11.5 and the *Rigveda* 10.13.1:
"Where fire is churned forth, where the wind is obstructed, and where the Soma overflows—there the mind is born. (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 2.6)
May one delight in the ancient prayer through the impulse of Savitṛ;
for you do not overlook that womb which you have prepared, nor has anything prior to it reached you.

Holding the body steady with its three parts erect, having withdrawn the senses into the heart by means of the mind, the wise man should cross over all perilous streams by means of the boat of Brahman. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.8)
Having restrained the vital breaths here with controlled exertion, one should breathe through the nostrils when the breath is exhausted;
like a chariot yoked to vicious horses, the wise man, remaining vigilant, should steady this mind. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.9)

In a clean place, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, which is agreeable to the mind and not distressing to the eyes due to the presence of sounds or bodies of water, one should practice in a cave or a sheltered spot protected from the wind. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.10)
Mist, smoke, the sun, wind, fire, fireflies, lightning, crystal, and the moon—these are the forms that precede the manifestation of Brahman in yoga. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.11)

When the fivefold quality of yoga has arisen from earth, water, fire, air, and space, and is fully operative, for him who has attained a body consisting of the fire of yoga, there is neither disease, nor old age, nor death. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.12)

Lightness of body, health, freedom from greed, clarity of complexion, excellence of voice, a pleasant odor, and scantiness of urine and feces—they say these are the first signs of the onset of yoga. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.13)

Just as a statue made of clay and plastered with lime shines forth brilliantly when well-burnt by fire, so too the embodied soul, having clearly perceived the reality of the Self, becomes solitary, fulfilled, and free from sorrow. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.14)

But when one who is disciplined perceives here the reality of Brahman through the reality of the self—likened to a lamp—as unborn, eternal, and purified of all principles, having known that God, he is released from all bonds. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.15)
This very God pervades all directions; he was born first, and he is within the womb.
He is the one already born, and he is the one yet to be born; facing every direction, he stands before all people with faces turned everywhere. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.16)

The god who is in the fire, who is in the waters, who has entered the entire world, who is in the plants, and who is in the trees—to that god, salutation after salutation. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 2.17)
Thus ends the second chapter.
The third chapter:
He who alone, possessing a net, rules by his ruling powers, rules all worlds by his ruling powers.
He who is indeed the one in both arising and existence—those who know this become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.1)

For there is only one Rudra; no second stood by him. He who rules these worlds with his ruling powers stands facing all people; having created all beings, he, the protector, withdraws them at the time of the end. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.2)

With eyes on all sides and a face on all sides, with arms on all sides and feet on all sides, the one God, generating heaven and earth, fans them together with his arms and wings. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.3)
This mantra is also found in Yajurveda 17.19 and Ṛgveda 10.82.3:
"He who is the source and the origin of the gods, the sovereign lord of all, Rudra, the great seer."
He who in the beginning generated Hiraṇyagarbha—may He endow us with auspicious understanding. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.4)
O Rudra, that auspicious form of yours which is not terrible and reveals no evil—with that most peaceful form, O Lord of the Mountain, look upon us with favor. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.5)
[*8] Yajurveda 16.2:

O Lord of the Mountain, with those [arrows] which you hold in your hand to discharge, O Protector of the Mountain, make them auspicious; do not harm the person or the world. [*9] Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.6.

[*9] Yajurveda 16.3. Thereafter, having known that supreme Brahman, the supreme Great One, who is hidden in all beings according to their respective forms, the one Lord who encompasses the universe—they become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.7)
I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness.
Only by knowing him does one pass over death; there is no other path for the journey. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.8)

[*10] Yajurveda 31.8: That than which there is nothing higher, than which nothing smaller or greater exists; like an immovable tree, He stands alone in heaven. By that Puruṣa, all this is pervaded. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.9)
That which is higher than that is formless and free from suffering;
those who know this become immortal, while others go only to suffering. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.10)
Having all faces, heads, and necks, dwelling in the secret cave of all beings, that Blessed Lord pervades everything; therefore, Śiva is omnipresent. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.11)
The Great Lord, the Puruṣa, is indeed the instigator of this being;
the Sovereign, the imperishable light, has attained this utterly stainless state. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.12)

The Person, the size of a thumb, the inner self, is ever seated in the hearts of men. He is conceived by the heart, by intuition, and by the mind; those who know this become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.13)
The Lord of Thought, the Puruṣa with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet,
having pervaded the earth on every side, stands beyond it by the measure of ten fingers. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.14)
The Person alone is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be; moreover, he is the lord of immortality, which transcends that which grows by means of food. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.15)

[*12] Yajurveda 31.1–2, Ṛgveda 10.90.1–2, Atharvaveda 19.6.1, 4. With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, with ears everywhere in the world, It stands encompassing all. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.16)
Appearing with the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all senses;
the Lord and Ruler of all, the vast refuge of all. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.17)
The embodied being, a friend, like a swan, flutters outside the city of nine gates;
he is the master of the entire world, both the stationary and the moving. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.18)
Handless and footless, yet swift and a grasper; he sees without eyes and hears without ears.
He knows that which is to be known, yet there is no knower of him. Him they call the foremost, the great Puruṣa. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19)
Smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest, the Self is hidden in the secret cave of this living being;
through the grace of the Creator, one who is free from desire beholds Him, the Lord, the Greatness. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.20)
[14] See KaṭhaU 1.2.20:
"I know this undecaying, ancient one, the Self of all, who has gone everywhere because of his omnipresence;
for those who discourse on Brahman indeed proclaim him eternally as the cessation of birth. (ŚvetUp 3.21)
Thus ends the third chapter.
The fourth chapter:
He who, being one and colorless, through the application of his manifold powers, bestows many colors according to their respective purposes.
He awakens all at the end and all at the beginning; may that God unite us with auspicious understanding. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.1)
That indeed is fire, that is the sun, that is the wind, and that is the moon;
that indeed is the pure, that is Brahman, that is the waters, and that is Prajāpati. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.2)

[*15] Yajurveda 32.1. You are female, you are male; you are a youth or even a maiden. You, as an old man, totter along with a staff; you are born facing in every direction. [*16] Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.3.

The blue-winged bird, green, red-eyed, containing lightning within, the seasons, and the oceans— you exist as the beginningless one through your omnipresence, from whom all worlds have been born. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.4) [Atharva-veda 10.8.27]
There is one unborn female (aja), red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form;
one unborn male (aja) lies beside her, delighting in her, while another unborn male leaves her after he has enjoyed her pleasures. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5)
Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree.
One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other looks on without eating. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6)

[*17] Atharva-veda 9.14.20, Ṛgveda 1.164.20. Clinging to the same tree, man is immersed and grieves, deluded by his lack of sovereignty. But when he perceives the other, the Lord who is cherished, and His majesty, then he is freed from sorrow. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.7)

In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest heaven, upon which all the gods have settled—what will he do with the Ṛgveda who does not know that? But those who know it, they sit here together. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.8)

The meters, the sacrifices, the rituals, the vows, the past, the future, and that which the Vedas declare—the Magician creates all this; and another, bound by his magic power (*māyā*), is confined within him. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.9)
One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā;
by his constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10)

He who alone presides over every womb, in whom all this world comes together and dissolves—having perceived that Lord, the boon-bestowing God, worthy of praise, one attains this ultimate peace. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.11)

May he who is the source and origin of the gods, the sovereign of all, Rudra the great seer—may he, beholding Hiraṇyagarbha as he is being born, endow us with auspicious understanding. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.12)

He who is the sovereign lord of the gods, upon whom the worlds are supported, he who rules over these bipeds and quadrupeds—to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation? (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.13)

Having known Him who is subtler than the subtlest, the creator of the manifold-formed world from within its chaotic mass, the one who encompasses the universe—having known that auspicious One, he attains ultimate peace. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.14)
[19] See below 5.13.
He alone is the protector of the world at all times, the Lord of all, hidden within all beings;
in whom the Brahman-sages and the deities are united. Knowing him thus, one cuts the bonds of death. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.15)

Having known Śiva, who is subtler than the cream upon clarified butter, hidden within all beings, and having known the God as the one enveloper of the universe, one is released from all bonds. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.16)
This divine Viśvakarman, the Great Self, is eternally seated within the hearts of all people.
He is fashioned by the heart, by insight, and by the mind; those who know this become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.17)
When there was darkness, that was neither day nor night, neither being nor non-being; Śiva alone existed.
That is the Imperishable, that is the most excellent splendor of Savitṛ, and from it the ancient wisdom issued forth. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.18)
Neither above, nor across, nor in the middle can one grasp him; there is no likeness of him whose name is Great Glory. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.19)
His form does not stand within the range of sight; no one beholds him with the eye.
Those who know him thus, as abiding in the heart by means of the heart and the mind, become immortal. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.20)
Thinking "He is unborn," a certain fearful person takes refuge [in you];
O Rudra, protect me forever with that face of yours which is the southern one. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.21)
Do not harm us in our children or grandchildren, nor in our life-span; do not harm us in our cattle or our horses.
O Rudra, do not slay our heroes in your wrath. Bearing oblations, we ever invoke you. (SvetU 4.22)
[*20] Yajurveda 16.16, Rigveda 10.114.8. Thus ends the fourth chapter; [now begins] the fifth chapter.
Two syllables, supreme and infinite, are Brahman, wherein knowledge and ignorance lie hidden;
ignorance is indeed the perishable, while knowledge is the immortal. He who rules over both knowledge and ignorance is another. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.1)
He who alone presides over every womb, over all forms and all wombs;
he who in the beginning sustains with his wisdoms the seer Kapila when born, and beholds him as he is being born. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.2)
Manifesting each single net in many ways, this God withdraws them into this field;
having created them again, the Great-Souled Lord, as their ruler, exercises sovereign authority over all. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.3)

Just as the sun shines, illuminating all directions—above, below, and across—so does that one, exalted, and venerable Lord preside over the natures of the sources of being. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.4)
And that which, as the source of the universe, ripens its own nature and transforms all things to be ripened;
that which alone presides over this entire universe and assigns all the qualities their respective functions. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.5)
That which is hidden in the secret Upaniṣads of the Vedas—Brahmā knows that as the source of Brahman;
those gods and seers of old who knew it became truly immortal, being absorbed in that. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.6)

He who is associated with the qualities (guṇas), who is the agent of actions that bear fruit, and the enjoyer of what he has done—he, possessing all forms, consisting of the three qualities, following the three paths, and being the lord of the vital breaths, wanders about according to his own deeds. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.7)
He who is the size of a thumb, whose form is like the sun, and who is endowed with volition and egoism;
by the quality of the intellect and by his own quality, he is seen as another, even the size of the tip of an awl. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.8)
If the tip of a hair is divided into a hundred parts, and each of those parts is again divided into a hundred, the living being (jīva) should be known as one such part; yet it is capable of infinity.
This is neither female nor male, nor indeed is it neuter;
whatever body it assumes, by that it is joined.

Through delusions of imagination, touch, and sight, the embodied soul, following its karma, sequentially attains various forms in different states of existence, arising from food, water, and rain as its means of growth. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.11)
The embodied soul assumes many forms, both gross and subtle, through its own qualities;
and another cause for their conjunction is also observed, namely, the qualities of action and the qualities of the self. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.12)

Having known the God—who is without beginning or end, who dwells in the midst of the chaotic mass, who is the creator of the universe and possesses manifold forms, and who alone encompasses the entire universe—one is released from all fetters. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.13)

Those who know the God—who is grasped through meditative state, called the "nestless," the auspicious one who brings about both existence and non-existence, and who effects the creation of the *kalās*—they have abandoned the body. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.14)
Thus ends the fifth chapter.
The sixth chapter:
Some poets, being utterly deluded, declare that it is inherent nature; others likewise say it is time.
This is the majesty of the God in the world, by which this wheel of Brahman is made to revolve.
By him indeed all this is eternally pervaded—he who is the Knower, the Ordainer of Time, the possessor of qualities, and the All-Knowing;
impelled by him, the action consisting of earth, water, fire, air, and ether revolves—this is to be meditated upon. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.2)

Having performed that action and having turned back from it again, one attains union with reality through reality, by means of one, two, three, or eight factors—namely, time and the subtle qualities of the self. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.3)

He who initiates actions endowed with qualities and employs all states of being—when those [actions] cease, there is the destruction of performed karma; upon the exhaustion of karma, he goes to that which is truly other. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.4)
He is the beginning, the cause and motive for conjunction; though partless, He is seen as transcending the three periods of time.
Having first worshipped that God, who is the soul of all beings, whose form is the universe, who is worthy of praise, and who abides within one's own mind—Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.5.

Knowing Him who is beyond this phenomenal world that revolves through trees, time, and forms; who brings forth dharma, dispels evil, is the Lord of fortune, the immortal Self abiding within, and the abode of the universe—[one attains immortality]. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.6)

Let us know Him, the God, the Lord of the world, worthy of praise—the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme deity among deities, and the supreme master among masters, beyond all others. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7)
For Him there exists neither effect nor instrument; neither one equal to Him nor superior to Him is seen.
His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are innate. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8)
He has no master in the world, nor any ruler, nor even any mark; He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses, and there is no progenitor of Him, nor any overlord. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9)

May that one God, who by his own nature veils himself with the products of primordial matter (pradhāna) as a spider does with its threads, grant us absorption into Brahman. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.10)
The One God is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner self of all beings;
He is the overseer of actions, the dwelling place of all beings, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11)

He is the one controller of the many inactive ones; he who makes the single seed manifold—those wise ones who perceive him abiding within themselves attain eternal happiness, and no others. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.12)

The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of the many—having known that Cause, the God who is attainable through Sāṅkhya and Yoga, one is released from all fetters. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13)

There the sun does not shine, nor do the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this earthly fire. It is only by His shining that everything shines after Him; by His light all this is illumined. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14)
There is one swan in the midst of this world; he alone is Agni, seated within the waters.
Knowing him alone, one goes beyond death; there is no other path for the journey. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.15)
He is the creator of all, the knower of all, whose source is the Self; he is the wise one, the master of time, possessed of attributes, and the knower of all.
He is the Lord of Pradhāna and the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña), the Master of the Guṇas, and the cause of liberation from, subsistence in, and bondage within saṃsāra. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.16)
Consisting of that, immortal, established in the Lord, he is the knower, all-pervading, and the protector of this world;
for he who eternally rules this universe—no other cause exists for his lordship. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.17)

I, seeking liberation, take refuge in that God who alone ordains Brahmā in the beginning and who indeed imparts the Vedas to him—He who is the light of the self's own intellect. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.18)
Partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless;
the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire that has consumed its fuel. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19)
When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather, then, without having known God, there will be an end to suffering. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.20)

Then the wise Śvetāśvatara, through the power of his austerity and by the grace of the gods, proclaimed to those beyond the stages of life this supreme purifier, which is cherished by the assembly of seers. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.21)
This supreme secret, taught in the Vedānta, was proclaimed in a former age;
it must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor again to one who is not a son or a disciple. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.22)
For that high-souled one who has supreme devotion to the Divine, and as toward the Divine, so toward the Guru—for him these truths thus taught indeed shine forth clearly. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23)
Oṃ. May He protect us both; may He nourish us both; may we work together with vigor;
may our study be brilliant; may we not harbor mutual hatred. Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace!
Thus ends the sixth chapter.
Thus the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is complete.
